lead.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on the PC’s Graphical Future
lead.dek: Bill Gates unveils a mouse-driven graphical layer for MS-DOS machines, promising menus, tiled windows and a common face for the compatible-computer boom.
body: NEW YORK, Nov. 10 — Microsoft this week unveiled Windows, a graphical operating environment intended to place menus, pictures and mouse control above the command-line face of MS-DOS. Bill Gates presented the product at the Helmsley Palace Hotel, giving the fast-growing world of IBM-compatible computers a glimpse of a more visual way to work.

The project began inside Microsoft under the working name Interface Manager. Its announced design combines pull-down menus, tiled windows, device-independent graphics and cooperative multitasking, allowing several programs to remain available within a shared screen environment.

Windows enters a field already being defined by Apple’s Lisa and VisiCorp’s Visi On. Microsoft’s wager is that a common graphical layer can span the many machines built around DOS, easing differences among displays, printers and pointing devices for both programmers and users.

The company is aiming for an April 1984 delivery, though the ambitious software remains unfinished. For buyers accustomed to typed commands, the announcement is still consequential: the largest supplier of microcomputer software has declared that the mouse and graphical desktop belong in the PC’s future.

Whether Windows arrives on schedule or wins immediate acceptance is uncertain. Yet this week’s demonstration has put a name on Microsoft’s strategy—and opened a contest over who will define the everyday face of personal computing.

stories.headline: A Self-Replicating Program Earns a New Name: Computer Virus
stories.dek: Fred Cohen’s controlled university demonstration exposes a new class of security problem.
body: At a Lehigh University computer-security seminar on November 10, graduate student Fred Cohen demonstrated a program able to attach itself to other programs and reproduce. The controlled experiment was academic research, not a public outbreak.

Cohen’s work gives the problem a memorable name—computer virus—and argues that shared systems can permit infections to spread with alarming speed. The demonstration adds a new concern to a year already filled with debate over unauthorized computer access.
The lesson is defensive: system designers must consider not only intruders but software that turns trusted programs into carriers. No operational code or intrusion instructions are reproduced here.

stories.headline: Computer Magazines Ride the Home-Micro Boom
stories.dek: Thick issues, machine-specific titles and type-in programs turn the magazine rack into a software shelf.
body: The New York Times reported November 9 on the explosive growth of computer magazines, a publishing boom fed by millions of new microcomputer owners seeking reviews, buying advice and programs.

General titles such as Byte, Creative Computing and Compute! share the rack with publications devoted to particular machines. Type-in listings make the magazines a low-cost distribution channel as well as reading matter.
Compute!’s November issue runs beyond 300 pages, its advertisements and product notices mapping an industry in which games, utilities and peripherals compete for the holiday buyer’s attention.

stories.headline: IBM-Hitachi Settlement Reported Near $300 Million
stories.dek: A reported secret pact underscores the value—and danger—surrounding mainframe compatibility.
body: A November 9 report said Hitachi agreed to pay IBM about $300 million to settle litigation accusing the Japanese company of technology theft.

The dispute grew from an FBI sting concerning alleged acquisition of IBM computer secrets. Its reported price shows how fiercely mainframe makers guard the engineering knowledge behind compatible systems.

undergroundDesk.headline: A Virus Is Named in a Controlled Security Test
undergroundDesk.dek: Academic research at Lehigh demonstrates self-replicating software without unleashing a public outbreak.
body: Fred Cohen’s November 10 seminar demonstration showed that software could attach itself to other programs and make them carriers in turn.
The controlled experiment belongs to computer-security research, not crime. It warns operators of shared systems that trusted programs can become a channel for rapid infection.
